title: Prosecutor v. Gotovina and Markač — artillery attacks on Krajina towns
question: Has it been established beyond reasonable doubt that the artillery attacks on Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac and Gračac were unlawful?
facts: From at least July 1995 to about 30 September 1995, Croatian leaders and officials initiated Operation Storm, a military action aimed at taking control of territory in the Krajina region of Croatia. Ante Gotovina was a colonel-general in the Croatian army, commander of its Split Military District, and overall operational commander of Operation Storm in the southern part of the Krajina. Mladen Markač was assistant minister of the interior and operational commander of the special police in Croatia. Artillery was used against Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gračac. The Trial Chamber analysed individual artillery impact sites in the four towns. It applied a 200-metre margin of error to all impact sites in each of the four towns and treated sites more than 200 metres from a target it considered legitimate as evidence of an unlawful attack. The Trial Chamber noted that it had not received sufficient evidence to make findings about wind speed and air temperature for each of the four towns. It found that the HV could not identify targets of opportunity, such as moving police or military vehicles, in the four towns. Expert witnesses testified about factors including wind speed and air temperature that could affect the accuracy of the weapons used. The record also included evidence about targets of opportunity in Knin. The Trial Chamber found that large numbers of civilians departed the Krajina region.
holding: In its Appeals Judgment of 16 November 2012, the ICTY Appeals Chamber reversed the Trial Chamber's finding that the artillery attacks on Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gračac were unlawful. Judges Agius and Pocar dissented from this conclusion. The Chamber also reversed the convictions of Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač and entered acquittals under Counts 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9.
key_reasoning: The Trial Chamber's 200-metre range-of-error standard was not linked to the evidence it received and was applied uniformly to impact sites in all four towns.
The trial record included evidence of targets of opportunity in Knin that the Trial Chamber had not clearly discounted.
The impact analysis could not be sustained, and the remaining evidence was insufficient to support a finding that the artillery attacks on the four towns were unlawful.
The Appeals Chamber concluded that no reasonable Trial Chamber could find beyond reasonable doubt that the four towns were subject to unlawful artillery attacks.
